werk/take-that-take-that-en-party.text:
In 1989 manager Nigel Martin-Smith built a boy band around the young singer and songwriter Gary Barlow, modelled on New Kids on the Block. The first single, Do What U Like, reached only number 82, but it brought the group to the attention of RCA. Promises and Once You've Tasted Love did not do well either. Only their cover of It Only Takes a Minute reached number 7 in the UK chart. I Found Heaven, A Million Love Songs and a cover of Could It Be Magic, with Robbie Williams on lead vocals, followed.

The debut album was released in August 1992 and reached number two in the UK album chart. It stayed in the top 75 for almost a year and a half and won Best Album at the Smash Hits Awards. The sound alternates between dance-oriented pop songs, covers and ballads.
werk/take-that-take-that-en-party.listen: Listen to the melody of A Million Love Songs: Gary Barlow wrote it when he was fifteen.

werk/talk-talk-laughing-stock.text:
After Spirit of Eden, bassist Paul Webb left the group in 1990, which turned Talk Talk into a duo of Mark Hollis and drummer Lee Harris. After a legal dispute they were free of EMI and signed with Polydor, which released the record on the jazz label Verve. From September 1990 to April 1991 they worked at Wessex Sound Studios in London, with producer Tim Friese-Greene and engineer Phill Brown. Verve provided money and freedom. The sessions were gruelling: the windows were covered up and the clocks taken off the walls, and guest musicians improvised without hearing the whole song. Most of the recorded material was thrown away.

The record has six tracks that together sound like one long piece, full of small gestures and shifting moods. Critics called it a landmark for the young post-rock scene. Pitchfork later gave it a 10, and in 2007 Stylus Magazine named it the best post-rock album. After its release the band broke up.
werk/talk-talk-laughing-stock.listen: Listen to Myrrhman, the opening track, and notice how quiet and sparse the music begins and how much space is left between the sounds.

werk/talking-heads-77.text: On 16 September 1977 the first Talking Heads album was released. The band played at CBGB but sounded very different from the Ramones: nervous, clever and danceable. Singer David Byrne and the others had met at art school. Bassist Tina Weymouth played bare, tight bass lines. In the 1980s they increasingly turned to funk and African rhythms.
werk/talking-heads-77.listen: Psycho Killer runs on a bare bass line built around the note A. Part of the lyrics is in French.

werk/talking-heads-fear-of-music.text:
After the performance of Take Me to the River on American Bandstand, Talking Heads did not want to be seen as a singles machine. In the spring of 1979 the band began without a producer, but the results were not satisfying. So Brian Eno was brought back. In April and May 1979 a Record Plant recording truck stood outside the apartment of Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth in Queens, with cables running through the window to the loft. The basic tracks were made there.

The album mixes disco rhythms, cinematic soundscapes and rock. David Byrne placed his characters only in dystopian situations, above all in Life During Wartime, inspired by his life on Avenue A in New York. I Zimbra opens the record with Afrobeat, disco, guitar work by Robert Fripp and a lyric based on a Dada poem by Hugo Ball. Critics praised the unconventional rhythms and the singing.
werk/talking-heads-fear-of-music.listen: Listen to I Zimbra. The lyrics seem like nonsense: can you hear how the rhythms take over the meaning?

werk/talking-heads-little-creatures.text:
Little Creatures is the sixth studio album by Talking Heads and was released in June 1985 on Sire Records. On this record the band looks at America itself: the lyrics are about American life, and the music takes elements from country music, with pedal steel guitar on many tracks. Eric Weissberg plays that guitar, on Creatures of Love and Walk It Down among others. Accordion, washboard and backing vocals also give the songs a playful, ordinary sound.

The critics of The Village Voice voted the record album of the year in the Pazz & Jop poll. It is the band's best-selling studio album, with more than two million copies sold in the United States. The cover was made by the outsider artist Howard Finster and was chosen by Rolling Stone as cover of the year.
werk/talking-heads-little-creatures.listen: Listen to the accordion and the washboard in Road to Nowhere, and notice how such a simple sound gives the song an old-fashioned, festive character.

werk/talking-heads-more-songs-about-buil.text:
This second Talking Heads album was released on 14 July 1978 on Sire Records. It was the first of three consecutive albums produced by Brian Eno. The band became noticeably more danceable on it: singer David Byrne's idiosyncratic delivery was given more support by the rhythm of bassist Tina Weymouth and drummer Chris Frantz. For the cover the band made a mosaic of 529 close-ups of Polaroid photographs, and the back shows a satellite photograph of the United States.

The only single was an adaptation of Al Green's Take Me to the River, the band's first song in the American top thirty. The critic Robert Christgau praised the tension between Byrne's compulsive outbursts and the supple rhythmic foundation. The album made the band a group that critics widely admired, and it ranked in NME's top four of 1978.
werk/talking-heads-more-songs-about-buil.listen: Listen to the bass and drums in Take Me to the River, and above them to David Byrne's remarkable singing. How do they work together?

werk/talking-heads-naked.text:
Naked, from 1988, is the eighth and last studio album by Talking Heads. After the straightforward pop songs of Little Creatures and True Stories, the band wanted something different. They travelled to Paris to work with producer Steve Lillywhite and international musicians, including Johnny Marr and Kirsty MacColl. Beforehand the band had already recorded about forty improvised tracks. In Paris they played all day and chose the best take at the end of each day. Lyrics and melodies followed only later, in New York.

The result mixes Afrobeat, Latin funk and art pop, with a warm, organic and percussive sound, deliberately different from the bombastic production of the 1980s. David Byrne said that many of the songs are about people without pretensions, which is why there is a chimpanzee on the cover. Critics saw a return to old form. The album reached number three in Great Britain. After that the band went on hiatus.
werk/talking-heads-naked.listen: Listen to Blind, the opening track, and notice the warm, percussive sound, full of rhythm.

werk/talking-heads-remain-in-light.text:
After Fear of Music, Talking Heads and producer Brian Eno wanted to show that the band was more than a backing group for singer David Byrne. In 1980 they went to Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas. There they played long instrumental jams, with the Nigerian musician Fela Kuti as a model. African polyrhythms and funk were mixed with electronics, and the instrumental tracks consisted of repeating loops. Guest musicians included guitarist Adrian Belew and singer Nona Hendryx. Byrne suffered from writer's block and wrote his lyrics as a stream of thoughts.

The album was released on 8 October 1980. Critics praised the experiments, the new rhythms and the way such different styles became a whole. Once in a Lifetime and Houses in Motion were released as singles. The record is often regarded as the band's high point and has been in the American National Recording Registry since 2017.
werk/talking-heads-remain-in-light.listen: Listen to Once in a Lifetime. Notice the repeating groove beneath the song and how the vocals sound like a stream of thoughts.

werk/talking-heads-speaking-in-tongues.text:
After the departure of producer Brian Eno and a short break, during which the band members worked on their own projects, recording of this album began in 1982. It was released on 1 June 1983 and became the band's commercial breakthrough. Burning Down the House reached number nine in the American chart, the band's only song in the top ten. The record also reached number two in the dance charts. Singer David Byrne designed the cover himself, and he partly explained the title by saying that he first sang nonsense and then made words to fit it.

Critics noted that the extra musicians made the sound more spacious, with gospel influences in Slippery People and Swamp. The lyrics remained impressionistic, but the music sounded light and danceable. A Rolling Stone reviewer wrote that the album erases the dividing line between artistic white pop and black funk. The tour was captured in the concert film Stop Making Sense.
werk/talking-heads-speaking-in-tongues.listen: Listen to Burning Down the House. Notice how danceable the song is, while the singer's lyrics are anything but clear.

werk/talking-heads-true-stories.text:
This seventh Talking Heads album was released in September 1986, shortly before singer David Byrne's satirical musical film True Stories. The record contains only studio recordings by the band of songs from the film. A soundtrack album with the actors did not appear until 2018. Wild Wild Life became the biggest hit and won two MTV Video Music Awards in 1987 with its video. Love for Sale also got a video, made for the film.

The music is more melodic than on the records before it. One reviewer called it gently melodic pop with little of the band's aggressive polyrhythms of those years, although he found some songs banal. He called Love for Sale and People Like Us fine rock music. In Hey Now a school choir sings along, and People Like Us gets a violin and pedal steel. The English band Radiohead named themselves after the song Radio Head.
werk/talking-heads-true-stories.listen: Listen to the primary-school choir that sings along in Hey Now, and notice how children's voices give the pop song an unusual colour.

werk/tangerine-dream-alpha-centauri.text:
Alpha Centauri is the second album by Tangerine Dream and was released in March 1971 on Ohr. The group sounded different from the debut, Electronic Meditation. There was more room for keyboards and electronics, although these still stayed in the background. The leading roles went to organ and flute. Edgar Froese himself called the atmosphere Kosmische Musik.

A Head Heritage reviewer wrote that the album used Pink Floyd's space rock template but drained the rock out of it. The single Ultima Thule had already been released in February 1971. It uses the same guitar riff as Fly and Collision of Comas Sola and was otherwise a stand-alone release. Later reissues in the 2000s added both parts of it as bonus tracks. The album sold 20,000 copies in Germany, almost four times as many as the later Phaedra.
werk/tangerine-dream-alpha-centauri.listen: Listen to Alpha Centauri and notice which instruments shape the atmosphere. Can you hear mostly organ and flute, and how spacious that sounds?

werk/tangerine-dream-electronic-meditati.text:
The debut by Tangerine Dream was released in June 1970 on the German label Ohr. The band recorded it in October 1969 in a rented factory in Berlin, with nothing more than a two-track Revox tape recorder. It is the only album with Edgar Froese, Klaus Schulze and Conrad Schnitzler together. Schulze left before the release, and Schnitzler shortly afterwards.

The music lies somewhere between free jazz, electronic art music and instrumental rock. Guitar, organ, drums and cello sound alongside home-built electronics and found sounds, such as breaking glass, burning parchment and peas being shaken through a sieve. At the end of side B there are reversed voices: Froese reads out the back of a ferry ticket. Journey Through a Burning Brain recalls the free improvisations of Schnitzler's Kluster. Critics call the record a cult curiosity, but also a landmark from which a whole universe of sound grew. The striking sleeve design originally included a balloon.
werk/tangerine-dream-electronic-meditati.listen: Listen to Journey Through a Burning Brain and notice the sounds that do not seem to come from ordinary instruments. Hear how the musicians improvise freely, without a fixed rhythm or melody.

werk/tangerine-dream-phaedra.text:
Richard Branson heard recordings that Edgar Froese and Christopher Franke had made in Berlin and gave the group a contract with Virgin. With the advance they bought a modular Moog synthesizer. Recording began in November 1973 at The Manor in Oxfordshire, and the album was finished in less than six weeks. Everything went wrong: the tape recorder broke down, the mixing desk gave up and the speakers were damaged by the low bass notes. After twelve days came a breakthrough.

This is the first record with the sound that later became so well known: the Moog sequencer as a driving bass guitar. In the title track the oscillators drift out of tune from the heat, which changes the music towards the end. Mysterious Semblance at the Strand of Nightmares was recorded in one take on a Mellotron. The album reached number fifteen in England with hardly any airplay and is regarded as a landmark of electronic music.
werk/tangerine-dream-phaedra.listen: Listen to the pulsing sequencer line in Phaedra that serves as a bass guitar, and notice how the sounds slowly change towards the end.

werk/tangerine-dream-zeit.text:
Zeit was released in August 1972 on the German label Ohr as a double album, the third by Tangerine Dream. It was the first record with Peter Baumann, alongside Christopher Franke and Edgar Froese. The subtitle is Largo in Four Movements. Florian Fricke of Popol Vuh plays Moog synthesizer, and four cellists open the first piece. The cover shows a solar eclipse. The music fits the idea behind the title: time in fact stands still and exists only in our heads.

The sound is slower and more atmospheric than on earlier records. One theme literally melts into the next, almost like classical music. Critics often call Zeit one of the first examples of dark ambient. One review spoke of a monolithic and sombre album, the group's most difficult. Steven Wilson names it his favourite album of all time and the birth of ambient.
werk/tangerine-dream-zeit.listen: Listen to Birth of Liquid Plejades and notice the cellists at the start and how the sounds slowly flow into one another.

werk/taylor-swift-1989.text:
Until her fourth album, Red, Taylor Swift saw herself as a country musician. On her fifth album she opted wholeheartedly for pop. She began writing in 2013, during the Red Tour, and wanted a coherent sound: if you chase two rabbits, you lose them both. In 2014 she moved from Nashville to New York. The title refers to her year of birth and to the synth-pop of the 1980s, with Annie Lennox and Peter Gabriel as inspiration. Max Martin, Shellback and Jack Antonoff co-produced.

The album was released on 27 October 2014. It sounds dense with synthesizers and drum machines, without the acoustic arrangements of the past. Shake It Off, Blank Space and Bad Blood became number ones on the American Hot 100. The reviews praised the production and the lyrics, although some felt the synth-pop displaced her singer-songwriter side. 1989 won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 2016.
werk/taylor-swift-1989.listen: Listen to Blank Space and notice how the sparse, electronic production and the tight rhythms give the lyrics room.

werk/taylor-swift-folklore.text:
Taylor Swift had planned a tour for April 2020, but it was cancelled because of the coronavirus pandemic. In quarantine she watched and read a lot of fiction. That led her to invented stories and characters instead of her usual autobiographical writing. She recorded her vocals in a home studio in Los Angeles and worked remotely with the producers Aaron Dessner and Jack Antonoff, who exchanged digital files with her. The album was released as a surprise on 24 July 2020.

It sounds calm, with piano, strings, orchestration and restrained percussion, in styles such as indie folk and chamber pop. The songs cardigan, the 1 and exile with Bon Iver reached the top ten internationally, and cardigan became number 1 on the American Hot 100. It was the best-selling album of 2020 in the United States. Critics praised the emotional depth and the rich lyrics. It won Album of the Year at the Grammys, making her the first woman to win that prize three times.
werk/taylor-swift-folklore.listen: Listen to exile (feat. Bon Iver) and notice the two voices: the song is a duet in which Justin Vernon of Bon Iver sings the male part.

werk/taylor-swift-midnights.text:
Taylor Swift announced Midnights at the 2022 MTV Video Music Awards. The album was released on 21 October, after folklore, evermore and her re-recordings of older albums. She called it a concept album about sleepless nights, with five themes: self-loathing, revenge fantasies, wondering what might have been, falling in love and falling apart. She made it with Jack Antonoff, in his studio Rough Customer in Brooklyn and at Electric Lady Studios in Manhattan.

It sounds minimalist and electronic: analogue synthesizers, sparse drum machine rhythms and processed vocals. It is described as synth-pop, electropop and dream pop. On Midnight Rain and Labyrinth her voice is pitched down. Anti-Hero, about insecurity and fame, became a number 1 in the United States. The album topped the American chart with more than a million copies in its first week and won Album of the Year at the 2024 Grammys, a first for the same artist for the fourth time.
werk/taylor-swift-midnights.listen: Listen to Midnight Rain and notice the voice: it is pitched down and therefore sounds low, to critics almost masculine or androgynous.

werk/taylor-swift-speak-now.text:
After the success of Fearless, Taylor Swift began on the next album straight away. She wrote it in 2009 and 2010 on tour, entirely on her own, because there was no co-writer on the road. The record is a loose concept album about things she still wanted to say to certain people. With producer Nathan Chapman she mixed country pop, country rock and power pop, with acoustic instruments, ringing electric guitars and strings.

Back to December asks an ex for forgiveness. In Speak Now the protagonist disrupts a wedding. Mean was about her critics and won a Grammy for Best Country Song. The album spent six weeks at the top of the Billboard 200. Critics praised the melodies and the emotion, although some found the confrontational songs superficial.
werk/taylor-swift-speak-now.listen: Listen to Mean and notice how the lyrics address an opponent directly.

werk/teach-in-ding-a-dong.text: On 22 March 1975 Teach-In from Enschede won the Eurovision Song Contest in Stockholm with Ding-a-dong, sung by Getty Kaspers. It was the fourth Dutch victory, and for a long time the last. The cheerful song also became a hit outside the Netherlands, in England among other places, just as ABBA had a year earlier with Waterloo. After that it took 44 years before the Netherlands won again.
werk/teach-in-ding-a-dong.listen: Ding-a-dong is a bouncy pop song with a chorus that can be sung along to in any language.

werk/television-marquee-moon.text:
In the mid-1970s Television was one of New York's leading groups, with a regular spot at the club CBGB. Demos that Brian Eno made in 1974 did not please Tom Verlaine: he found them too cold and brittle. In August 1976 the band signed with Elektra, which let Verlaine produce, assisted by engineer Andy Johns. The recording took place in New York in November 1976, after weeks of rehearsals of four to six hours a day.

Verlaine and guitarist Richard Lloyd left the power chords of punk behind and chose interplay, melodic lines and countermelodies, with influences from rock and jazz. The lyrics are about youth, discovery and rapture, with references to Lower Manhattan. The record received wide praise and was unexpectedly successful in the United Kingdom.
werk/television-marquee-moon.listen: Listen to Marquee Moon and notice how the two guitars alternate melodic lines and countermelodies, instead of just strumming chords.

werk/tems-born-in-the-wild.text:
Tems became internationally known through Essence with Wizkid and co-wrote Rihanna's Lift Me Up. Her debut album had been announced for before 2023 but was a long time coming. In March 2024 she said that it was finished. At Coachella she had already played Love Me JeJe, the first song to be released. The album was released on 7 June 2024 and has eighteen tracks, including two interludes. Tems co-produced it herself, with GuiltyBeatz, Sarz and P2J among others. J. Cole and Asake are guests.

NME heard the rich diversity of West Africa in the music, from highlife to hip hop. Pitchfork called it adventurous and melancholy. In the United States it became the highest-ever chart position for a Nigerian female singer. Love Me JeJe won a Grammy for Best African Music Performance, and the album was nominated for Best Global Music Album.
werk/tems-born-in-the-wild.listen: Listen to the soft, velvety singing on Hold On, the closing track. Notice how calmly the album ends with it.

werk/terence-blanchard-romantic-defiance.text:
Romantic Defiance was released on 30 May 1995 on Columbia. It is a studio album by the American jazz trumpeter Terence Blanchard and contains eight lyrical original compositions. He plays in a quintet with pianist Edward Simon, bassist Chris Thomas, drummer Troy Davis and tenor saxophonist Kenny Garrett, for whom it was a debut on tenor.

The album was well received. Billboard called it a strong, searching quintet record. Peter Watrous of The New York Times wrote that the group is exceptionally aware of dynamics and evokes a sense of calm in long quiet passages. Brian Morton and Richard Cook called the album wonderful in their Penguin Jazz Guide.
werk/terence-blanchard-romantic-defiance.listen: Listen to Romantic Defiance and notice the lyrical melody and how Kenny Garrett's tenor saxophone complements the quintet.

werk/terence-blanchard-simply-stated.text:
Simply Stated was Terence Blanchard's second album as a bandleader. Columbia Records released it on 5 May 1992. Blanchard described the record as a love letter to Miles Davis. It contains four well-known jazz standards and four originals. The musicians included Sam Newsome on tenor saxophone, Bruce Barth on piano and Rodney Whitaker on double bass.

The album reached the top ten of the Billboard traditional jazz chart. Nick Deriso of Something Else found the record pleasant but never truly triumphant, and named Dear Old Stockholm and When It's Sleepytime Down South as its strong points. For him it was the beginning of Blanchard's growth from young lion to modern benchmark. Scott Yanow of AllMusic found Blanchard in top form and called the record strongly connected to hard bop, yet fresh.
werk/terence-blanchard-simply-stated.listen: Listen to Dear Old Stockholm, a song associated with Miles Davis, and notice how the trumpet plays the melody.

werk/terence-blanchard-terence-blanchard.text:
This was the first album on which Terence Blanchard was heard as a bandleader. Columbia Records released it on 18 June 1991. Delfeayo Marsalis produced it. Branford Marsalis and Sam Newsome played tenor saxophone, Bruce Barth piano. Before that, Blanchard had worked on the film Mo' Better Blues, as arranger, trumpeter and trumpet teacher to the actor Denzel Washington.

The album opens and closes with a hymn: Motherless Child and Amazing Grace. In between are four originals and three standards. Scott Yanow of AllMusic wrote that Blanchard was ready to become one of the great trumpeters of the 1990s. Leonard Feather praised Tomorrow's Just a Luxury and Sing Soweto as proof of a strong compositional talent, but found Wandering Wonder and Azania somewhat too exuberant.
werk/terence-blanchard-terence-blanchard.listen: Listen to Motherless Child, which opens the record, and notice how a hymn immediately sets the tone of the album.

werk/terence-blanchard-the-malcolm-x-jaz.text:
The Malcolm X Jazz Suite was released on 20 April 1993 on Columbia. Terence Blanchard wrote and orchestrated the music for Spike Lee's last two films up to that point, Jungle Fever and Malcolm X. For this album he chose the strongest themes from the second film and arranged them for a jazz quintet. Bassist Tarus Mateen, tenor saxophonist Sam Newsome, pianist Bruce Barth and drummer Troy Davis had also played on the film score.

Critics were enthusiastic. Scott Yanow of AllMusic called it one of his best records and felt that the music stands up on its own, apart from the film. David Hajdu of Entertainment Weekly heard influences of the reflective, modal jazz that Miles Davis made in the time of Malcolm X's rise. In 1994 the album was nominated for a Soul Train Music Award.
werk/terence-blanchard-the-malcolm-x-jaz.listen: Listen to Malcolm's Theme and notice how a theme from the film is worked out here by a jazz quintet.

werk/thad-jones-after-hours.text:
After Starboy in 2016, The Weeknd wanted to take a different path. In January 2019 he tweeted no more daytime music, and at the end of 2019 the singles Heartless and Blinding Lights followed. The album was released on 20 March 2020. He produced it largely himself, with Max Martin, Metro Boomin, Illangelo and OPN among others. He borrowed the title from Martin Scorsese's 1985 film. About its content he said that these are thoughts from three to five o'clock at night, after the club and after arguments.

The music is synth-pop and new wave with dream pop, R&B and synthwave, and the lyrics are about loneliness, self-loathing, escape and regret. Heartless and Blinding Lights became number 1 on the American Hot 100, and the album went straight to the top of the Billboard 200. Critics praised the production and the cohesion and sometimes called it his best work. After Hours is the first part of a trilogy.
werk/thad-jones-after-hours.listen: Listen to Blinding Lights and notice how the glossy synthesizers and the tight drums give an upbeat sound to a lonely lyric.

werk/thad-jones-detroit-new-york-junctio.text:
This record was recorded on 13 March 1956 and released on Blue Note. The session was one of the first for pianist Tommy Flanagan after he had moved to New York. A day earlier he had played with the same rhythm section on a recording by guitarist Kenny Burrell. Besides the trumpeter Thad Jones we hear tenor saxophonist Billy Mitchell, Burrell, bassist Oscar Pettiford and drummer Shadow Wilson.

Little Girl Blue is an exception, because only Jones, Burrell and Pettiford play on it. The rest of the record is a full line-up with piano, saxophone and drums. A later AllMusic reviewer called it an excellent set of driving hard bop, the solid, constantly moving jazz style of those years.
werk/thad-jones-detroit-new-york-junctio.listen: Listen to Little Girl Blue and notice the small line-up without piano and drums. Note how this gives the trumpet more room.

werk/the-alan-parsons-project-eve.text:
Eve is the fourth studio album by the Alan Parsons Project, released on 27 August 1979 by Arista. The plan was at first an album about great women from history, but it grew into a broader record about the strength of women and the problems they encounter in a man's world. Chris Rainbow sang with the group for the first time, and the sleeve is by Hipgnosis.

The opening instrumental Lucifer became a big hit in Europe and is the theme tune of the German TV programme Monitor. Damned If I Do reached the American top 40. At the beginning you hear Morse code that Parsons picked up from shortwave radio without knowing what it said. Singers such as Clare Torry and Lesley Duncan, who were also heard on The Dark Side of the Moon, share the lead parts. Critics praised the production. Parsons later said that the record was criticised for supposedly being too macho.
werk/the-alan-parsons-project-eve.listen: Listen to Lucifer and notice the Morse code signal at the start and how the synthesizers then take over the song.

werk/the-alan-parsons-project-i-robot.text:
In 1977 the Alan Parsons Project made its second album, loosely based on Isaac Asimov's robot stories. Eric Woolfson spoke with Asimov himself, who was enthusiastic. However, the rights already belonged to a film and television company, so the comma disappeared from the title and the theme and lyrics became more general: the rise of the machine and the fall of man. The album was released in July. It came, by coincidence, just after Star Wars, at a time when robots were popular.

The sound is layered and smooth, with a vocoder that Billboard said recalled Kraftwerk and Tangerine Dream. Some Other Time got its title because Paul McCartney had turned down a request with those words. Jaki Whitren and Peter Straker sing together on it. Singles were I Wouldn't Want to Be Like You, Don't Let It Show and Day After Day. The sleeve is by Hipgnosis. The reviews were mixed, but mostly favourable.
werk/the-alan-parsons-project-i-robot.listen: Listen to I Robot and notice the vocoder and the electronic sounds. Try to hear how the studio itself is used as an instrument.

werk/the-allman-brothers-band-brothers-a.text:
After the death of Duane Allman in 1971 and the success of Eat a Peach, the Allman Brothers Band bought a farm in Juliette, Georgia. Bassist Berry Oakley visibly suffered from the loss and was killed in a motorcycle accident in November 1972. Chuck Leavell joined on piano and Lamar Williams on bass. Dickey Betts took over the role of bandleader, and many of his compositions sounded more country. The album was recorded largely over three months in Macon, co-produced by Johnny Sandlin.

Brothers and Sisters was released on 6 August 1973 and became the band's commercial high point: more than seven million copies worldwide. Ramblin' Man reached number two on the American Hot 100, the group's only top-ten hit.
werk/the-allman-brothers-band-brothers-a.listen: Listen to Ramblin' Man and notice what the guitars and the vocals do: can you hear the country sound of Betts?

werk/the-allman-brothers-band-eat-a-peac.text:
After their breakthrough with the live album At Fillmore East, the Allman Brothers Band began work on a third studio album in 1971. On 29 October 1971 guitarist and bandleader Duane Allman was killed in a motorcycle accident in Macon. Eat a Peach became his last album. It is a double album of studio recordings from Criteria Studios in Miami, with and without Duane, and live recordings from the Fillmore East, produced by Tom Dowd.

Mountain Jam lasts half an hour and fills two sides of the original double LP. Gregg Allman sings Melissa, his brother's favourite song, and Dickey Betts's Blue Sky became a staple of classic rock radio. The title comes from a remark by Duane Allman about a peach for peace. The album was an immediate success, reached number four on the American chart and went platinum.
werk/the-allman-brothers-band-eat-a-peac.listen: Listen to Melissa and notice how Gregg Allman sings his brother's song: what does the voice do to the atmosphere?

werk/the-allman-brothers-band-idlewild-s.text:
After a debut that was commercially not very successful, the band toured the United States in 1969 and 1970. The second album was made between gigs, over five months, in studios in Macon, Miami and New York. Tom Dowd, who had already been planned for the debut, now did become the producer. The band recorded most of it live, with all the musicians at the same time. The title refers to a wooden cabin outside Macon, where the group rehearsed and partied.

The album contains two of the group's best-known songs. Midnight Rider is a ballad that later became a solo hit for Gregg Allman. In Memory of Elizabeth Reed is an instrumental that became a fixture of the concerts. On release in 1970 the album sold modestly, but sales grew thanks to more than three hundred performances. AllMusic later called it the group's best studio album, and Rolling Stone saw it as a step towards a new kind of Southern music.
werk/the-allman-brothers-band-idlewild-s.listen: Listen to In Memory of Elizabeth Reed: follow how the two guitars alternate and how the organ and drums lay a jazz-like foundation beneath them.

werk/the-allman-brothers-band-the-allman.text:
The debut came about in 1969, after guitarist Duane Allman had put together a band in Jacksonville with two guitarists and two drummers. His brother Gregg became the singer. In August the group recorded the album at Atlantic Studios in New York, under the direction of staff engineer Adrian Barber, because producer Tom Dowd was not available. Recording and mixing took two weeks. The band had already played the songs live for months, so they were firmly in place.

The sound mixes blues, jazz and country. Dreams shows the jazz influence, and Whipping Post became a crowd favourite. Trouble No More and Don't Want You No More are adaptations of existing songs. The album initially sold poorly, but Rolling Stone called it subtle, honest and moving. Later Dowd made a new mix, because the band did not like Barber's original mix.
werk/the-allman-brothers-band-the-allman.listen: Listen to Dreams: notice the slide guitar solo, which Duane Allman improvised in the dark after the session, and hear how atmospheric it sounds.

werk/the-bad-plus-these-are-the-vistas.text:
This second album by the American piano trio The Bad Plus was the first on a major label, Columbia Records. Pianist Ethan Iverson, bassist Reid Anderson and drummer David King were given Tchad Blake as producer, who came from the world of Los Lobos, Tom Waits and Pearl Jam. According to JazzTimes he listened above all to the friction between acoustic instruments.

The result sounds both big and bare. The Wall Street Journal spoke of a jazz power trio with a rock and roll heart. You can see that in three adaptations of pop songs: Smells Like Teen Spirit by Nirvana, Heart of Glass by Blondie and Flim by Aphex Twin. For many listeners this was the first introduction to the group. In 2009 NPR counted the album among the fifty most important recordings of the decade.
werk/the-bad-plus-these-are-the-vistas.listen: Listen to Smells Like Teen Spirit: hear how the piano takes over Nirvana's vocal line and how bass and drums lay a rhythm of their own, jazz-like, beneath it.

werk/the-band-music-from-big-pink.text:
In 1967 Rick Danko, Richard Manuel, Garth Hudson, Robbie Robertson and Levon Helm, then still known as Bob Dylan's backing band, played in the basement of a pink house in West Saugerties, New York. There they also wrote songs of their own. That house, Big Pink, gave the debut album its name. In early 1968 they recorded the record with producer John Simon in New York and Los Angeles. Asked how it should sound, they answered: exactly like in the basement.

The sound mixes country, rock, folk, R&B and soul and was recorded live, without overdubs. The cover is a painting by Dylan, who also wrote one song and co-wrote two. Reviewers, including Al Kooper in Rolling Stone, praised the record. It was released in July 1968 and showed the group as a voice of its own alongside the psychedelia of the time. Eric Clapton cites the album as a reason for leaving Cream.
werk/the-band-music-from-big-pink.listen: Listen to The Weight and notice how the different singers take turns. The sound is raw and organic, because the band recorded it live.

werk/the-band-the-band.text:
After a failed attempt at a studio in New York, the group set up in the poolhouse attached to a rented house in the Hollywood Hills in Los Angeles. The house had previously belonged to Sammy Davis Jr. and Judy Garland. Guitarist Robbie Robertson chose the spot to give the songs the loose atmosphere of the Basement Tapes, a clubhouse idea. John Simon produced, and the last three songs were recorded after all at The Hit Factory in New York. It was the band's second album.

The songs are about people, places and traditions from an old-fashioned America, and the album is therefore sometimes called a concept album. The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down and King Harvest (Has Surely Come) draw on history. The critic Robert Christgau had expected little but found the record better than Abbey Road. In 2003 Rolling Stone ranked the album number 45 on its list of the greatest albums of all time.
werk/the-band-the-band.listen: Listen to Jawbone, which was written in the unusual time signature of 6/4. Try to feel how the rhythm just stops you from tapping along as in an ordinary rock song.

werk/the-beach-boys-little-deuce-coupe.text:
Little Deuce Coupe was released on 7 October 1963 on Capitol Records, three weeks after Surfer Girl. It is the Beach Boys' fourth album and the first whose title has nothing to do with surfing. The theme is hot rods and cars, which is why it counts as one of the first rock concept albums. Four songs had already appeared on earlier records. The eight new songs were recorded in a hurry, but Brian Wilson's arrangements became more and more complicated, especially in No-Go Showboat and Custom Machine. It was the last record with guitarist David Marks until 2012.

The title refers to a 1932 Ford Coupe, for many enthusiasts the ultimate hot rod. The photo on the cover came from Hot Rod magazine and shows the car of its owner, Clarence Catallo. Be True to Your School was re-recorded for a single and became a hit again.
werk/the-beach-boys-little-deuce-coupe.listen: Listen to No-Go Showboat and notice the harmonies. Hear how layered the arrangement is compared with a simple car song.

werk/the-beach-boys-pet-sounds.text:
Brian Wilson stopped touring in early 1965 to concentrate on writing and studio work. For this eleventh album he wrote the songs with lyricist Tony Asher and arranged and produced everything himself. He wanted to build further on Phil Spector's Wall of Sound and to surpass the Beatles' Rubber Soul. Recording ran mainly from January to April 1966. Studio musicians, among them the Wrecking Crew, largely took over the instruments from the band, while the layered vocal harmonies remained the core.

The sound combines pop with jazz, classical influences, found sounds and instruments that were unusual in rock. The lyrics are personal: You Still Believe in Me is about one's own shortcomings and I Just Wasn't Made for These Times about alienation. In the United States the reception was lukewarm, in Great Britain enthusiastic. Later Pet Sounds was called one of the most influential albums ever.
werk/the-beach-boys-pet-sounds.listen: Listen to I Just Wasn't Made for These Times and notice the contrasts between the soft, vulnerable singing and the rich arrangements around it.

werk/the-beach-boys-surf-s-up.text:
After the disappointing Sunflower, the band looked for a new image in 1970. New manager Jack Rieley had the matching stage suits abolished, made Carl Wilson the official leader and gave the group a new social tone. Recording ran from January to July 1971. Brian Wilson was less active in the studio than before, which is why the vocal arrangements sound thinner.

The lyrics more often deal with the environment, society and health. Carl Wilson contributed major songs for the first time, Long Promised Road and Feel Flows. The album is named after the closing track Surf's Up, which was originally intended for the unfinished album Smile. The title and the sleeve, with a painting after a sculpture called End of the Trail, nod to the earlier surf image. The album received mostly good reviews and reached number twenty-nine in the United States, higher than the group had reached with new work since 1967.
werk/the-beach-boys-surf-s-up.listen: Listen to Surf's Up and notice how the song changes mood and how the voices come together at the end.

werk/the-beach-boys-surfer-girl.text:
Surfer Girl was released on 16 September 1963 on Capitol Records, after Surfin' U.S.A. had made the group one of the biggest in America. That success gave Brian Wilson the room to do the production himself, something that was not yet done in the music industry. He worked from May to July at Western Studio in Hollywood. Al Jardine, who had earlier been replaced, returned to the band during the recording.

The album consists largely of surf songs. For the first time strings are heard, in The Surfer Moon, and session musicians of the Wrecking Crew play, in Hawaii and Our Car Club. Wilson called Catch a Wave his first major vocal arrangement. The AllMusic reviewer singled out In My Room as the most important song. A music historian saw in the record a step forward in Wilson's growth as a composer and producer.
werk/the-beach-boys-surfer-girl.listen: Listen to In My Room and notice how soft and personal this song sounds beside the surf songs around it.

werk/the-beach-boys-surfin-safari.text:
The Beach Boys' debut album was released on 1 October 1962 on Capitol Records. The group came largely from Hawthorne, California. The success of the single Surfin' Safari made Capitol want a whole album. In the studio Brian Wilson fought for control of the production and got it, even though it was not in the credits. He wrote or co-wrote nine of the twelve songs.

There are short, playful songs about surfing, cars and girls. On 409 you hear recordings of a car driving past the Wilsons' house. The instrumental Moon Dawg was regarded as the first surf record. Surfin' was later credited with starting the California Sound genre, and 409 with the hot rod craze of the 1960s. One reviewer found most of the songs mediocre, but the record does show how the band itself sounded in the studio.
werk/the-beach-boys-surfin-safari.listen: Listen to 409 and notice the sounds of a real car between the vocals. Hear how the song uses the engines as an instrument.

werk/the-beat-i-just-can-t-stop-it.text:
I Just Can’t Stop It is the debut album by The Beat, an English Two-Tone band from Birmingham. It was released on 23 May 1980 on Go-Feet Records. In the United States it came out on Sire under the name The English Beat, with Tears of a Clown and Ranking Full Stop added, two songs that had been released in 1979 as a double A-side on 2 Tone. Bob Sargeant produced the record. The girl on the sleeve, the Beat Girl, was drawn by the cartoonist Hunt Emerson.

The band played with singer Dave Wakeling, toaster Ranking Roger and saxophonist Saxa. Rolling Stone found the music wild and menacing, sexy and sharp. At the end of 1980 the album ranked high in the year-end lists of NME, Sounds and OOR. Simon Reynolds counts it among the five most important albums of the Two-Tone and ska revival. Mirror in the Bathroom and Twist & Crawl are still highly regarded.
werk/the-beat-i-just-can-t-stop-it.listen: Listen to the rhythm guitar in Mirror in the Bathroom and the ska rhythm that carries the nervous vocals.

werk/the-beatles-a-hard-day-s-night.text:
In the spring of 1964 the Beatles recorded their third album, around the shooting of their first feature film. During a break Ringo Starr came up with the expression a hard day's night, which became the title of the film. Lennon and McCartney wrote a song for it that was recorded at EMI Studios on 16 April. The first side of the record contains the film music, the second side songs that were written for the film but did not make it in. It is the first album consisting entirely of original songs by Lennon and McCartney.

The rock 'n' roll covers of earlier records are gone, replaced by short, lively pop songs with layered vocals, direct choruses and subtle accompaniment. On several songs George Harrison plays a Rickenbacker twelve-string guitar, a sound that influenced the Byrds and other folk rock bands. The title song, with its distinctive opening chord, and Can't Buy Me Love were number one on both sides of the Atlantic.
werk/the-beatles-a-hard-day-s-night.listen: Listen to the title song A Hard Day's Night and notice the opening chord, and then hear how the twelve-string guitar colours the rest of the song.

werk/the-beatles-abbey-road.text:
After the tense sessions for Get Back, Paul McCartney suggested to producer George Martin that they make an album like the old days. Martin agreed, on condition that the group stuck to discipline. Recording ran mainly in April, July and August 1969. The mood was better than a year earlier with the White Album, but there were still conflicts, over Maxwell's Silver Hammer among other things, and John Lennon was absent for some songs. It was the last album the band recorded.

The sound mixes rock, pop, blues and progressive rock, with striking use of the Moog and of guitar through a Leslie speaker. On the second side a long medley of short songs runs together. George Harrison wrote Something and Here Comes the Sun, two of his best songs for the group. The first reviews were mixed, but later the album grew into one of the best of all time.
werk/the-beatles-abbey-road.listen: Listen to the second side, from You Never Give Me Your Money through to The End. Notice how the short songs flow into one another without a pause, like one long suite.

werk/the-beatles-beatles-for-sale.text:
Beatles for Sale was released on 4 December 1964, the fourth album by The Beatles within 21 months. The group came back exhausted from a year full of tours. Recording began in August at EMI Studios in London and continued during a British tour, and most of the writing was done in the studio. Producer George Martin later remarked that the band was war-weary.

The tone is quieter and gloomier than before. Only eight songs are original work by Lennon and McCartney; the rest are covers of Carl Perkins, Chuck Berry and Buddy Holly, among others. In No Reply and I'm a Loser John Lennon writes about himself, under the influence of Bob Dylan, whom the group had met in New York that year. Country also colours the sound. In the studio the band tried out new things: Eight Days a Week opens as the first pop song with a fade-in. In the United Kingdom the reviews were favourable.
werk/the-beatles-beatles-for-sale.listen: Listen to the start of Eight Days a Week: the song slowly builds up instead of starting at once. Try to hear how that feels different from an ordinary opening.

werk/the-beatles-help.text:
Help! is the Beatles' fifth album and the soundtrack of their second film, made by director Richard Lester. Recording began on 15 February 1965 with Ticket to Ride in Studio Two of EMI, after which the group flew to the Bahamas to film. Seven of the fourteen songs are in the film and fill the first side.

In the studio they kept layering multiple tracks on top of one another. On Yesterday a string quartet plays, the first time the group used baroque sounds, and You've Got to Hide Your Love Away has flutes. The record received favourable reviews. In the United States ordinary critics began to see the group as serious artists, and the album was nominated for a Grammy for Album of the Year, the first time a rock band was named in that category.
werk/the-beatles-help.listen: Listen to Yesterday and notice the role of the string quartet, and hear how sparse the accompaniment is compared with the rest of the record.

werk/the-beatles-let-it-be.text:
Paul McCartney intended the project as a return to the group's rock 'n' roll roots. In January 1969 rehearsals began at Twickenham for a TV documentary. The mood was bad, as a result of which George Harrison temporarily left. As a condition for his return they went to their own Apple Studio, with Billy Preston on keyboards. On 30 January came the concert on the roof of the studio, their last public performance. Glyn Johns's mixes were rejected, and the project was shelved while the band recorded Abbey Road.

In the end Phil Spector was commissioned to put the album together. He added orchestra and choir to The Long and Winding Road, among others, which offended McCartney. The album came out after the announcement that the band had split up. The reviews were bad at the time, but later opinion became more positive. In 2003 Let It Be... Naked was released without Spector's treatments.
werk/the-beatles-let-it-be.listen: Listen to The Long and Winding Road and notice the strings and the choir. This is the song whose treatment by Phil Spector caused so much quarrelling.

werk/the-beatles-magical-mystery-tour.text:
Magical Mystery Tour belongs to the television film of the same name from 1967. The idea came from Paul McCartney, who after Sgt. Pepper wanted to film a psychedelic bus trip. After the death of manager Brian Epstein at the end of August the project went ahead after all, and the recording ran alongside the filming and editing. Biographers call the sessions unfocused, and producer George Martin spoke of organised chaos. In England a double EP was released, in the United States an LP with extra singles.

The Beatles kept experimenting with the studio. For I Am the Walrus John Lennon sang through a poor microphone and the song got strings, horns and a choir with laughter and noises. George Harrison's Blue Jay Way uses reversed tape and a Leslie speaker. McCartney contributed The Fool on the Hill. The film received mixed reactions, but the music was a success: in America the album spent eight weeks at the top of the Billboard chart.
werk/the-beatles-magical-mystery-tour.listen: Listen to I Am the Walrus and notice Lennon's voice, which through a poor microphone sounds as if he comes from the moon. Can you also hear the strange sounds of the choir?

werk/the-beatles-please-please-me.text:
After their contract with EMI in May 1962, the Beatles ended up with George Martin at the label Parlophone. Their first single, Love Me Do, reached number 17, to Martin's surprise. He suggested making an album and, because the Cavern Club proved unsuitable for recording, chose an ordinary studio record. On 11 February 1963 the Beatles recorded almost the whole album in one day at EMI Studios. Later Martin added overdubs to Misery and Baby It's You, and the four songs from the earlier singles were included as well.

The record contains covers and original work by Lennon and McCartney. That band and songwriters were the same was unusual and marks the rise of the band that plays its own songs. In Great Britain the album stayed in the top 10 for more than a year, a record for a debut album. In the United States it was not released in this form. Critically it is still held in high regard.
werk/the-beatles-please-please-me.listen: Listen to I Saw Her Standing There and notice how energetic and tight a band sounds that recorded this album in one day.

werk/the-beatles-revolver.text:
After Rubber Soul, in early 1966 the Beatles were given, for the first time in years, a long break of three months without obligations. That gave them an unprecedented amount of time to prepare a new album. Because they did not want to play these songs live, they made full use of the studio: double-tracked vocals, tapes running backwards, altered speeds and instruments that did not belong to their live line-up.

Eleanor Rigby has only a string octet as accompaniment and is about loneliness. Love You To brings Hindustani classical music into pop. Tomorrow Never Knows combines a heavy Indian drone with a collage of tape loops. The album was released on 5 August 1966 with Eleanor Rigby and Yellow Submarine on one single. It is regarded as one of the greatest and most innovative albums in pop history, and many critics now think it better than Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band.
werk/the-beatles-revolver.listen: Listen to the drone in Tomorrow Never Knows that sounds through almost the whole song, and to the strange sounds that pop up in between.

werk/the-beatles-rubber-soul.text:
For the first time the Beatles were allowed to record an album without obligations for concerts, radio or film. Recording at EMI Studios in London began on 12 October 1965 and lasted four weeks. Most of the songs came about after that summer's American tour, where the band met Bob Dylan and heard Motown and Stax on the radio. After A Hard Day's Night it was only the second album with original songs only.

The sound is softer and more varied than before, with influences of pop, soul and folk and with new instruments such as sitar, harmonium and fuzz bass. The lyrics became more mature, especially those of John Lennon. The title refers to the notion of plastic soul, the way the group acknowledged being less authentic than the soul artists they admired. The album received much praise, shifted attention from singles to complete albums and was later regarded as a key work for psychedelia and progressive rock.
werk/the-beatles-rubber-soul.listen: Listen to Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) and notice the exotic twang of the sitar among the acoustic guitars: a new instrument in the Beatles' music.

werk/the-beatles-sgt-pepper.text:
At the end of August 1966 the Beatles stopped performing for good. During a flight to London in November Paul McCartney had the idea for a song about an Edwardian military band, and from that grew the idea for this album. The group continued the studio experiments of Revolver, now without a fixed deadline. Recording began on 24 November at EMI Studios and was finished on 21 April 1967. Strawberry Fields Forever and Penny Lane were released separately as a single.

With producer George Martin and sound engineer Geoff Emerick, many songs received sound effects and treated tape, such as Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds, Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite! and A Day in the Life. The styles range from music hall and circus to avant-garde and Indian music. The album was released on 26 May 1967 and won four Grammys in 1968, including Album of the Year. The sleeve was designed by Peter Blake and Jann Haworth.
werk/the-beatles-sgt-pepper.listen: Listen to A Day in the Life and notice the build-up to the final chord. Can you hear how the song shifts in mood between its different sections?

werk/the-beatles-yellow-submarine.text:
Yellow Submarine belongs to the 1968 animated film and was released in January 1969. For the band it was mainly a contractual obligation: United Artists wanted four new songs for the film, and the group, just finished with Sgt. Pepper, showed little enthusiasm. Some songs were recorded specially, others had been left over from earlier.

Only the first side contains songs by The Beatles themselves: four new ones, plus the previously released Yellow Submarine and All You Need Is Love. George Harrison's Only a Northern Song is about his dissatisfaction with the group's music publisher. John Lennon's Hey Bulldog ends with a jam that stayed in the final mix. The second side consists of orchestral music by George Martin, recorded with an orchestra of 41 musicians at Abbey Road. Critics reacted mixed: some felt that the album fell below the group's usual level.
werk/the-beatles-yellow-submarine.listen: Listen to the end of Hey Bulldog. Notice what happens after the point where the song could have faded out: the band lets loose for a little longer.

werk/the-blue-diamonds-ramona.text: In 1960 the Indo-Dutch brothers Riem and Ruud de Wolff, as The Blue Diamonds, had a big hit with Ramona, an old American song that they sang in two-part harmony, with soft guitars. In Germany it reached number one. It was one of the first big international successes of Dutch pop musicians. Indo-Dutch musicians were the first to show that Dutch people could make pop music for the world.
werk/the-blue-diamonds-ramona.listen: Hear how the two brothers sing exactly together, in thirds, like the Everly Brothers in America.

werk/the-byrds-ballad-of-easy-rider.text:
This album took its name from the title song, intended as the theme song of the 1969 film Easy Rider. Peter Fonda asked Bob Dylan for a song; he wrote a few lines on a napkin with the instruction to give them to McGuinn. Roger McGuinn finished the song. Dylan later had his name removed as co-writer. The film brought the band more attention, even though most of the music had nothing to do with it.

The recording sessions of July and August 1969 were led by Terry Melcher, whom the group brought back as producer after two earlier albums. It was the second album by the line-up with Clarence White, Gene Parsons and John York, who was fired shortly after it was finished. Besides the title song, Jesus Is Just Alright and Deportee stand out. The first reactions were mixed. Today it is regarded as one of the stronger records from the band's later years.
werk/the-byrds-ballad-of-easy-rider.listen: Listen to Ballad of Easy Rider and notice how the song fits the film as a theme, with a simple melody and a lyric about a river flowing to the sea.

werk/the-byrds-byrdmaniax.text:
Byrdmaniax was released in June 1971 on Columbia, as the tenth album by the Byrds. The group had just had success with Ballad of Easy Rider and (Untitled) and was touring without a break. Recording began in October 1970 under producer Terry Melcher, but the new songs were still barely worked out.

The album includes Pale Blue, a quiet acoustic ballad by Roger McGuinn and Gene Parsons, and I Trust, a gospel-like song. There are also light-hearted pieces, such as I Wanna Grow Up to Be a Politician, a ragtime-like song from the never-completed musical Gene Tryp, and the bluegrass instrumental Green Apple Quick Step. While the band was on tour, Melcher had strings, horns and a gospel choir laid over the songs, reportedly without the group's permission. The record was poorly received and the band members were themselves dissatisfied with it.
werk/the-byrds-byrdmaniax.listen: Listen to Pale Blue and notice the melancholy vocals and the simple acoustic instruments, which many critics regard as a lost classic.
